title: Healthcare Provider Guide to Medical Interpreter Services
summary: Everything healthcare providers need to know about medical interpreter services in July 2026 - from Section 1557 compliance to telehealth and
body_markdown:
###


The 2024 Section 1557 final rule requires covered entities to provide free, timely, qualified language assistance to patients with limited English proficiency, post annual notices in English and the 15 most common non-English languages in the state, and have any machine-translated content reviewed by a qualified human translator before patient delivery. Bilingual staff pressed into service do not meet the "qualified interpreter" standard for clinical decision encounters.


###


Yes. Under Section 1557 and Title VI, interpretation must be provided at no charge to the patient; the healthcare organization carries the expense. Medicaid reimburses interpretation in roughly 18 states, HRSA-funded FQHCs can direct 330 grant dollars toward language access, and Medi-Cal managed care plans may provide interpreter lines for enrolled members, but Medicare and most commercial payers do not reimburse it as a separately billable service.


###


Opalite works alongside qualified human interpreters, not in place of them. Healthcare organizations define approved use cases and set escalation rules that preserve human interpretation for informed consent, end-of-life discussions, psychiatric crises, and any encounter where the patient requests one. Opalite handles the high-volume, routine interactions where connection delays and per-minute costs create the most friction.


###


"Qualified" is a regulatory term requiring verified bilingual proficiency, formal training in medical terminology and interpreter ethics, and documented competency: not simply being fluent in two languages. The Certification Commission for Healthcare Interpreters offers the CoreCHI, CoreCHI-P, and language-specific CHI credentials; candidates must complete at least 40 hours of training and pass a scored exam. When a vendor claims certified interpreters, ask which credential, which certifying body, and what percentage of their active roster holds it.


###


Start with a language needs assessment using registration data to identify your top 15 languages plus rare requests, then score vendors on connection time by language, 24/7 coverage, HIPAA posture including a signed BAA and SOC 2 Type II report, EHR integration with Epic, Cerner, or eClinicalWorks, billing structure including silent-time charges, and verifiable interpreter credentials. A vendor that cannot answer connection-time or credential questions in writing is giving you the answer.
